From the surgery

Searching symptoms online

Being informed is good, but searching a symptom alone can take you from a headache to a tumour in three clicks. How to use the internet without feeding anxiety.

By Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

More and more people come to the surgery having first searched their symptoms online. There is nothing wrong with that in itself: being informed helps people ask better questions and take part in decisions. The problem arises when searching, instead of reassuring, feeds worry.

Why the internet is frightening

A study by Ryen White and Eric Horvitz of Microsoft analysed millions of searches and found that people who searched common symptoms, such as a headache, often ended up reading about rare and serious diseases. Search engines show what is read most and what alarms most, not what is most likely. And our minds give more weight to whatever is most frightening. This circle of searching, getting scared and searching again has been called cyberchondria.

When searching becomes a problem

If searches take up a lot of time, if worry increases after each one rather than decreasing, or if the same symptoms are searched again and again, searching has stopped informing and become a way of calming anxiety that, in the long run, keeps it going. It is similar to what happens when asking for tests to feel reassured.

How to make the internet work for you

  • Choose reliable sources: websites of scientific societies, the public health system or recognised patient associations.
  • Look for what is common, not everything that is possible: the usual causes of a symptom are usually the most likely.
  • Set a time limit and do not search at night.
  • Bring your questions to the appointment rather than keeping them to yourself: the doctor can judge what applies to you.
